extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on poetic diction, metaphor, word-formation, and the construction of plot and metre for tragedy and epic narrative (unity of action, scale, episodes, metre, narrator’s role, and the element of the wonderful). Draws on classical standards for appropriate diction by genre and for dramatic vs. narrative imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of a sentence or phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sentence or Phrase is a composite significant sound, some at least of whose parts are in themselves significant; it may form a unity in two ways—either as signifying one thing, or as consisting of several parts linked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentences/phrases that form a unity either by expressing a single unified idea (e.g. 'the definition of man') or by being a linked sequence of parts (e.g. the Iliad as a linked whole). A phrase need not contain a verb to be a unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of words and their forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these categories when choosing diction; they have different effects and suit different poetic ends. The text gives examples and morphological notes (lengthening by vowel change or insertion, contraction by removal, alteration by recasting part of the form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Current (proper) vs strange words (register & audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: A current or proper word is one which is in general use among a people; a strange word is one which is in use in another country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose current/proper words to ensure perspicuity for your intended audience; strange words may be used for distinction but will be foreign to the audience. The same word can be current for one people and strange for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and types of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy (proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor by transference (genus↔species, species↔species) or by proportional analogy; you may qualify a metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative. Metaphors can be used even when no ordinary word exists for a relation (e.g. 'sowing the god-created light').

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of coinage and altered forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one never even in local use but adopted by the poet; a word is lengthened when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or a syllable is inserted; contracted when part removed; altered when part remains and part is re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented, lengthened, contracted, or altered words can give distinction. Use such licenses sparingly to raise diction without sacrificing clarity; critics who condemn all such licenses err when they forbid their judicious use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: be clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; at the same time it is mean. That diction which is lofty is raised above the commonplace by employing unusual words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance: predominately current/proper words for clarity, supplemented by some unusual/ornamental/metaphorical terms to elevate style. Avoid styles that are entirely commonplace (mean) or entirely obscure (riddle or jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in employing poetic licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such license at all obtrusively is grotesque; but in any mode of poetic diction there must be moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use metaphors, strange words, lengthenings, or other devices obtrusively or for their own sake. Appropriate, restrained use produces distinction; overuse makes diction ludicrous or unreadable. Examples contrast Aeschylus and Euripides where one rare term alters perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of riddle and jargon (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of metaphors is a riddle; wholly of strange words is a jargon. The essence of a riddle is to express true facts under impossible combinations; a jargon results from strange terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make diction impenetrable by excessive metaphoric compression (riddle) or by excessive rarity/foreignness (jargon). Maintain a mix so the reader can perceive truth without being perplexed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as highest quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius, for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a natural faculty for recognizing likenesses; good metaphors require perception rather than learned technique. Prioritize metaphoric aptness and relevance over mere ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction (mapping words to genres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry all varieties are serviceable; in iambic verse the most appropriate words are those found even in prose (current/proper, metaphorical, ornamental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match word-forms to genre: use rare and elevated diction in heroic/epic contexts; use metaphors and familiar-speech diction in iambic (satirical/expressive) verse; dithyrambs favor compound formations. Consider meter and genre when selecting lexical register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity for narrative imitation (single action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing extended narrative in a single metre (epic or long narrative poems) ensure the core subject is one integrated action. Detach a manageable portion rather than attempting an entire vast subject; allow episodes but keep them subordinated to a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and scale (length limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view. This condition will be satisfied by poems on a smaller scale than the old epics, and answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose themes too vast to occupy a single organized whole; limit scope so the poem’s beginning and end can be comprehended as a unit. If theme is too large, it becomes unwieldy or over-complicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes and simultaneous events (epic advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Epic poetry many events simultaneously transacted can be presented; these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem and relieve the story with varying episodes. For sameness of incident soon produces satiety, and makes tragedies fail on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative form, employ relevant episodes and parallel events to add variety and grandeur. Use episodes to diversify and prevent monotony, but ensure their relevance to the main action so unity is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage plausibility and the limits of dramatic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: In Tragedy we cannot imitate several lines of actions carried on at one and the same time; we must confine ourselves to the action on the stage and the part taken by the players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for performance, ensure actions are plausible on stage; avoid scenes that would be absurd if enacted (e.g., an implausible pursuit where stage mechanics make characters behave ludicrously). What is plausible in narrative may be ludicrous in enacted drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre appropriate to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the metre, the heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience. If a narrative poem in any other metre or in many metres were now composed, it would be found incongruous. The iambic and trochaic tetrameter have different effects (trochaic akin to dancing, iambic expressive of action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heroic (stateliest/most massive) metre for epic narrative; avoid mixing different metres within a large-scale narrative. Choose metre that fits the tone and formal demands of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial restraint: minimal poet-narration
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator. Homer, after a few prefatory words, at once brings in a man, or woman, or other personage; none of them wanting in characteristic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatized speech and character action over overt authorial commentary. Let characters embody qualities; avoid excessive authorial intrusion which weakens imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The element of the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful depends for its chief effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry, because there the person acting is not seen. The wonderful is pleasing (audiences like added 'truths' or skilled lies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate the marvelous or extraordinary as appropriate to genre to increase audience pleasure, but manage it so it does not produce absurdity in performance. Use the wonderful to enhance interest—especially in narrative where logistical implausibilities are less noticeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural components: reversals, recognitions, and suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have... Reversals of the Situation, Recognitions, and Scenes of Suffering. Moreover, the thoughts and the diction must be artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your plot includes recognitions, reversals, and poignant scenes of suffering where appropriate; cultivate artistic thought and diction to render these moments effective. Song and spectacle are exceptions, but the core dramatic devices remain necessary.
